prompt.context: Our client, Bell Computer Inc., is the second largest PC manufacturer, by unit sales, in the United States. Over the past 5 years, Bell has been gaining market share and growing revenue, but at the same time, their net income is eroding. The founder of Bell has returned to the company and taken over as CEO. He has hired us to determine the cause of the profit margin decline and what can be done to improve profitability.
prompt.question: Why have Bell's profit margins declined? What can Bell do to improve its profitability and reach its 'Full Potential'?

clarifying_info.a: ASP stands for Average Selling Price — the average price at which the company sells a computer. Multiplying units sold by ASP gives total revenue.
PCs designed for and sold to retail consumers, either direct or through a retailer like Best Buy.

clarifying_info.q: Does Bell sell anything other than hardware?
clarifying_info.a: Assume that only hardware is sold as shown in the exhibits. (Note: selling additional items such as printers, software, warranty service, etc. could be explored as improvement ideas.)

clarifying_info.q: Is this a domestic or global analysis?
clarifying_info.a: This is a US domestic decision only. Ignore international.

clarifying_info.q: Do all competitors face the same pricing environment?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. All competitors face the same ASPs and sell comparable products.

exhibits.title: Product Mix Breakdown by Business Segment for 2005 and 2010
exhibits.shows: Two pie/bar charts comparing PC units (thousands) sold in 2005 vs. 2010 across product segments: Desktop PCs, Laptop PCs, Netbook PCs, Servers, and Other. Note: Netbook PCs did not exist in 2005. 'Other' products include Pocket PCs and Calculators.
exhibits.data: 2005 totals: Desktop 20K, Laptop 10K, Netbook 0K, Servers 5K, Other 5K (Total 40K). 2010 totals: Desktop 30K, Laptop 30K, Netbook 5K, Servers 10K, Other 5K (Total 80K).

exhibits.title: ASPs by Business Segment 2005 and 2010
exhibits.shows: A chart showing Average Selling Prices for each product segment in 2005 and 2010. Note: Netbook PCs did not exist in 2005.
exhibits.data: Desktop ASP: $1,000 (both years). Laptop ASP: $2,000 (2005) → $750 (2010). Netbook ASP: $500 (2010 only). Server ASP: $3,000 (both years). Other ASP: $250 (both years).

exhibits.title: Avg. Per Unit Cost Breakdown of a Desktop PC for Bell (2005, 2010) and Top 3 Competitors
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing per-unit cost breakdown (parts/CPU, direct labor, G&A, and other cost components) for Bell in 2005, Bell in 2010, and each of the top 3 competitors (Haysus, Racer, HC). Note: Servers, Laptops, and Netbooks have the same cost per unit as Desktops; 'Other' products have a total CPU of $200.
exhibits.data: Bell 2005 CPU per unit: $800. Bell 2010 CPU per unit: $800 (unchanged). Competitor best-in-class costs imply a combined CPU of ~$350 per unit (Haysus for parts, Racer for direct labor, HC for G&A). Other products CPU: $200 (unchanged across scenarios).

framework: Set up the Profit Equation: Profit/Unit = Price/Unit (ASP) – Variable Cost/Unit – Fixed Costs/Unit
Compare Bell's financials Before (FY2005) vs. After (FY2010): revenue is up and market share is growing, but net income is down
Diagnose: Are ASPs falling? (Exhibit 2) → Are units growing? (Exhibit 1) → Have costs kept pace? (Exhibit 3)
Identify root cause: product mix shift toward lower-ASP products + flat cost structure = margin erosion
Quantify the problem: calculate Net Income per unit, Revenue, Total Cost, and Net Income by product and in total for 2005 and 2010
Identify the 'Full Potential' cost benchmark: use competitor best practices to determine maximum achievable cost reduction
Quantify the opportunity: recalculate Net Income under full-potential costs
Formulate recommendation: copy best-in-class competitor costs to close the cost gap

questions.prompt: Calculate Net Income per unit, Total Revenue, Total Cost, and Total Net Income for Bell in FY2005 by product segment.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 1 (units) and Exhibit 2 (ASP) to compute revenue, subtract CPU of $800/unit (from Exhibit 3) to get NI/unit, then multiply by units to get segment and total figures. Key insight: all product margins were healthy in 2005.

math.setup: Revenue = Units × ASP; NI/Unit = ASP – CPU; Total NI = NI/Unit × Units
steps: Total Revenue = $56.25M; Total Cost = $29M; Total NI = $27.25M; Profit Margin ≈ 48.4%
math.answer: FY2005 Total Revenue ~$56.3M, Total NI ~$27.3M, overall profit margin ~48.4%.

questions.prompt: Calculate Net Income per unit, Total Revenue, Total Cost, and Total Net Income for Bell in FY2010 by product segment. What has changed?
questions.guidance: Same structure as FY2005 but now Laptop ASP has fallen to $750 (below the $800 CPU cost) and Netbooks at $500 ASP also lose money per unit. Desktops and Servers are still profitable. Revenue has grown but net income has fallen due to the mix shift toward money-losing segments.

math.setup: Revenue = Units × ASP; NI/Unit = ASP – CPU ($800 for all non-Other); Total NI = NI/Unit × Units
steps: Total Revenue = $86.25M; Total Cost = $61M; Total NI = $25.25M; Profit Margin ≈ 29.3%
math.answer: FY2010 Total Revenue ~$86.3M, Total NI ~$25.3M, overall profit margin ~29.3%. Revenue grew 53% but NI fell from $27.3M to $25.3M — a ~7% decline. Laptops and Netbooks are now money-losing per unit.

questions.prompt: Why have Bell's profit margins declined? Summarize the root cause.
questions.guidance: Candidate should synthesize three factors from the three exhibits: (1) product mix shifted toward Laptops and new Netbooks which represent a larger share of units; (2) Laptop ASPs fell from $2,000 to $750, and Netbook ASPs are only $500 — both below Bell's $800 cost per unit; (3) Bell has not reduced its cost per unit at all (still $800) while prices fell, so Laptops and Netbooks now generate negative margins. Servers remain highly profitable but the mix shift dilutes them.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, identify Bell's 'Full Potential' cost structure by benchmarking against competitors. Calculate Full Potential Net Income by segment and in total.
questions.guidance: Candidate should read Exhibit 3 to find that each of the top 3 competitors excels in a different cost component: Haysus has lowest parts/procurement cost, Racer has lowest direct labor, HC has lowest G&A. Adopting all three best practices implies a 'Full Potential' CPU of ~$350/unit (down from $800), reducing cost per box by $450. Then recalculate NI under these costs using 2010 units and ASPs.

math.setup: Full Potential CPU = ~$350 (best-in-class across competitors); NI/Unit = ASP – $350; Total NI = NI/Unit × Units; Cost reduction per box = $800 – $350 = $450
steps: Desktop: NI/unit = $1,000 – $350 = $650; 30K units; NI = $19.5M (up from $6M, improvement $13.5M)
Laptop: NI/unit = $750 – $350 = $400; 30K units; NI = $12M (up from –$1.5M, improvement $13.5M)
Netbook: NI/unit = $500 – $350 = $150; 5K units; NI = $0.75M (up from –$1.5M, improvement $2.25M)
Server: NI/unit = $3,000 – $350 = $2,650; 10K units; NI = $26.5M (up from $22M, improvement $4.5M)
Other: CPU unchanged at $200; NI = $0.25M (no change)
Total NI = $59M vs. $25.3M today; Total improvement ≈ $33.7M; Full Potential profit margin ≈ 68.4%
math.answer: Full Potential Total NI ~$59M, profit margin ~68.4%, representing a ~$34M improvement over FY2010 by cutting cost per box by $450 through competitor benchmarking.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond cost reduction, what other strategies could Bell pursue to improve its profitability?

categories.name: Cost reduction beyond benchmarking
ideas: SKU rationalization — reduce the number of product models to simplify manufacturing and procurement
Consolidate suppliers to gain volume discounts

categories.name: Pricing and mix management
ideas: Exit or minimize investment in money-losing Netbook segment
Emphasize Server segment which has 73%+ margins
Bundle products to increase average transaction value

categories.name: Revenue diversification
ideas: Enterprise/B2B sales which tend to have higher ASPs and stickier relationships
Financing/leasing programs to reduce price sensitivity

recommendation: Bell's margin decline is driven by a product mix shift toward Laptops and Netbooks whose ASPs have fallen below Bell's current $800 cost per unit, while costs have remained flat.

To reach Full Potential, Bell should immediately benchmark and adopt best-in-class cost practices from competitors: Haysus's parts procurement, Racer's direct labor model, and HC's G&A structure — reducing cost per box by $450 and improving total net income by ~$34M (to ~$59M at a ~68% margin).
risks: Implementing all three competitors' cost strategies simultaneously may be operationally complex and take time
Competitor cost structures may reflect different supplier relationships or geographies that are not easily replicable
Continued ASP declines in the industry could erode margins even after cost reductions
Exiting or de-emphasizing Netbooks could cede market share to competitors in a fast-growing segment
next_steps: Deep-dive into each cost component (parts, direct labor, G&A) to identify specific actions needed to match best-in-class levels
Assess feasibility and timeline for supplier renegotiation and manufacturing process changes
Evaluate whether to continue in the Netbook segment or manage it to profitability
Explore complementary high-margin product lines (printers, software, warranties) to diversify revenue
